subject: English
description: Personal, possessive, reflexive, relative pronouns; usage + errors

questions.explanation: POSSESSIVE PRONOUN (stand-alone, no noun follows): MINE, YOURS, HIS, HERS, ITS, OURS, THEIRS. Used after BE-verb or alone: 'The book is MINE'. POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE (modifies a following noun): MY, YOUR, HIS, HER, ITS, OUR, THEIR. Used before noun: 'My book' / 'her car'. INSIGHT — many languages don't distinguish possessive pronoun + adjective; English does. Common error: 'The book is MY' (wrong; 'my' needs a noun after it). Pronoun classification: PERSONAL (I, you, he); POSSESSIVE (mine; my); REFLEXIVE (myself); DEMONSTRATIVE (this, that); RELATIVE (who, which); INTERROGATIVE (who?); INDEFINITE (someone, anything).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'Between you and ___, the secret is safe.' (I / me)
questions.explanation: After PREPOSITIONS (between, for, to, with, etc.) → use OBJECT PRONOUN: ME, you, HIM, HER, IT, US, THEM. 'Between you and ME' (correct). Common HYPER-correction: people say 'between you and I' thinking 'I' sounds polite — actually WRONG. SUBJECT pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) used as SUBJECTS of clauses ('I am tired'). 'Between you + me' is on every grammar test. Other tricky cases: 'just for you and me' (NOT 'and I'); 'gave it to him and me' (NOT 'he and I'). Test: drop the other person → 'between me' (sounds right) vs 'between I' (sounds wrong).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'The man ___ called yesterday is my uncle.' (who / whom)
questions.explanation: WHO vs WHOM rule: WHO = subject (does the action); WHOM = object (receives action). 'WHO called' (he is the doer of calling). Compare: 'The man WHOM I called' = I called him; he is the OBJECT. SHORTCUT TEST: replace with HE/SHE (subject) or HIM/HER (object). 'HE called' fits → 'who'. 'I called HIM' fits → 'whom'. Modern usage: 'whom' is fading in conversational English; 'who' often replaces it. But formal writing + grammar tests still distinguish. WHOSE = possessive for both people + things ('the man whose car...'). WHICH = things only ('the car which...').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'Each of the boys has done ___ work.'
questions.explanation: INDEFINITE pronouns 'EACH', 'EVERY', 'ANY', 'EITHER', 'NEITHER' are SINGULAR — pronoun + verb agreement must be singular. 'Each of THE BOYS has done HIS work.' (his = singular possessive). Modern usage trend: 'their' for gender-neutrality has spread, but exam English typically expects 'his/her' or 'his'. Same for: 'EVERYONE has his own opinion' (formal); colloquially 'their own opinion' (gender-neutral). INSIGHT — 'each' grammatically singular even when followed by 'of + plural noun': 'each of THEM IS guilty' (NOT 'are').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'She did the work all by ___.'
questions.explanation: REFLEXIVE pronoun used when subject + object are SAME person, OR for emphasis. 'BY HERSELF' = alone, without help. List of reflexives: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. NOTE: ONESELF (not 'oneself's). Don't say: 'hisself' (wrong; correct = himself); 'theirselves' (wrong; correct = themselves). EMPHATIC use: 'I myself saw it' = I personally saw it (intensifier). REFLEXIVE: 'I cut myself' = I cut me (subject = object). Common use: 'enjoy yourself' (have fun), 'help yourself' (serve yourself food).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'Neither John nor his brothers ___ available.' (is / are)
questions.explanation: NEITHER ... NOR / EITHER ... OR — verb agrees with NEAREST subject (proximity rule). 'Brothers' (plural) is closest → 'ARE'. If reversed: 'Neither his brothers nor John IS available' (singular John closer). KEY RULES related to subject-verb agreement: (1) Singular subjects joined by 'AND' = plural verb ('John and Mary are'). (2) Joined by 'OR/NOR' = nearer subject's number. (3) 'Each, every, any, none, anybody, somebody' = singular. (4) 'Both, several, many' = plural. (5) Collective nouns (team, government) = singular if as a whole, plural if members ('The team is winning' / 'The team have their problems').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'Everyone is responsible for ___ own actions.' (his / their)
questions.explanation: Traditional / formal English: EVERYONE / EVERYBODY / SOMEONE = SINGULAR. Singular antecedent → singular pronoun: 'his' (or 'his/her' / 'his or her'). MODERN trend: SINGULAR THEY accepted for gender-neutrality — 'Everyone has THEIR own opinion'. Both used in 2020s+. EXAMS: typically expect 'his' (formal) — though increasingly accept singular 'they'. Style guides differ — APA, Chicago endorse singular 'they'; some PYQ banks still strict. SAME pronouns: anyone, anybody, no one, nobody, somebody, someone, each, none — all singular grammatically. INSIGHT — usage evolves; 'they' for unknown / non-binary singular antecedent is increasingly mainstream (Merriam-Webster 'word of year' 2019).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Was it ___ who forgot to attach the enclosures to the official letter?

options.option_text: him (object pronoun, follows prepositions and verbs)

questions.explanation: 'He' is correct because after 'It is/was', the complement takes the nominative (subject) form — 'It was he who forgot.' 'He' is the notional subject of the relative clause 'who forgot'. 'Him' is the most tempting distractor because it sounds natural in speech, but in formal/exam English the nominative case is required after 'it was'.

questions.stem: The warden handed the attendance register to both Meera and ___.

options.option_text: I (subject pronoun, used only as sentence subject)
me (object pronoun, correct object of preposition)
myself (reflexive pronoun, needs prior 'I' as antecedent)

questions.explanation: 'To' is a preposition; its object must be in the objective case — 'me'. 'I' (nominative) can only serve as a sentence subject. 'I' is the most tempting distractor because speakers often hypercorrect ('Meera and I'), but that rule applies only when the pair is the subject, not the object. 'Myself' requires 'I' earlier in the same clause as its antecedent.

questions.stem: ___ notebook containing the solved answer key was discovered on the invigilator's desk?

options.option_text: Who's (contraction standing for 'who is' or 'who has')
Whose (possessive interrogative pronoun modifying a noun)
Whom (objective case pronoun, cannot precede a noun)
Which (used for inanimate choices, not possession)

questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive form of 'who' and correctly modifies 'notebook'. 'Who's' is the most tempting distractor — it sounds identical when spoken — but 'who's' is a contraction of 'who is/has' and cannot act as a possessive determiner before a noun. Substitution test: 'Who is notebook was discovered' is nonsensical, confirming 'who's' is wrong.

questions.stem: Two interns, Aditi and ___, were shortlisted for the final interview at the district collectorate.

options.option_text: I (nominative, correct — appositive renames the subject)
me (objective pronoun, wrong case for subject position)
myself (reflexive, requires prior 'I' in the same clause)
mine (possessive pronoun, incorrect case entirely here)

questions.explanation: 'Aditi and ___' is an appositive phrase renaming the subject 'Two interns', so the nominative 'I' is required. Quick test: remove 'Aditi and' — 'I was shortlisted' is correct, confirming nominative case. 'Me' is the most tempting distractor because it follows 'Aditi and', which feels like an object position, but appositives mirror the case of the noun they rename.

questions.stem: The divisional commissioner distributed commendation letters to all of ___ — the officers, the clerks, and the field staff.

options.option_text: we (nominative subject pronoun, wrong after preposition)
our (attributive possessive, must precede and modify a noun)
us (objective pronoun, correct as object of preposition)
ourselves (reflexive pronoun, needs 'we' earlier in clause)

questions.explanation: 'Of' is a preposition; its object must be in the objective case — 'us'. 'We' is nominative and can only serve as a subject. 'We' is the most tempting distractor because the appositive list ('the officers, the clerks…') sounds like a subject inventory, but the governing word is still the preposition 'of'. 'Our' must always directly precede and modify a noun.

questions.stem: To ___ should the petition for reclassification of the tribal land be formally addressed?

options.option_text: who (nominative pronoun, used only in subject position)
whom (objective pronoun, correct object of preposition)
whomever (objective indefinite, implies any eligible person)
whoever (nominative indefinite, wrong case after preposition)

questions.explanation: 'To' is a preposition requiring the objective case — 'whom'. 'Who' is the classic tempting distractor: when the sentence is inverted ('To whom should…'), candidates mistake 'who' as the subject, but it is actually the object of 'to'. Substitution test: 'addressed to him' — 'him' confirms objective case, so 'whom' is correct. 'Whomever' is grammatically objective but implies any unknown person from a set, changing the meaning to an open-ended offer rather than a specific inquiry.

questions.stem: The Chief Auditor ___ scrutinised every ledger entry before the compliance report was submitted to the ministry.

options.option_text: him (objective pronoun, cannot intensify a clause subject)
his own (possessive phrase, must directly precede a noun)
he himself (double subject construction, ungrammatical here)

questions.explanation: 'Himself' here is an emphatic (intensifier) pronoun, not reflexive — it stresses that the Chief Auditor personally performed the action. Emphatic pronouns can be dropped without altering core meaning. 'Him' is the most tempting distractor but is objective case and cannot intensify a subject. 'He himself' is the common overcorrection — adding 'he' creates an awkward double-subject. The key examiner test: emphatic vs. reflexive is distinguished by whether the pronoun could be removed (emphatic = yes; reflexive = no, as it changes meaning).
